raw_case_text: A 28-year-old Indian male with chronic weakness, loss of appetite, and a pulsatile mass in the abdomen was referred to our department for radiological evaluation. The patient was normotensive, non-smoker, non-diabetic, and was admitted for alteration of his general state, including weight loss, dizziness, and mild fever (38 C) for past 1 month. Laboratory evaluation evidenced elevated white cell count [20,000 per cubic mm (normal 3000-11,000)] and C-reactive protein (CRP). Tuberculin skin test was positive. Blood culture result was negative for Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species, Salmonella, Gram-negative bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas mycobacterium, and fungi, such as C. albicans and Aspergillus. The patient had no history of tuberculosis or any previous intravascular procedure. Abdominal ultrasound (USG) showed mild hepatosplenomegaly and multiple significantly enlarged, heterogeneous, necrotic, conglomerate retroperitoneal lymph nodes including periportal and peripancreatic nodes. Color flow Doppler examination demonstrated multiple variable-sized aneurysms of abdominal aorta with pulsatile flow in the center and thrombus at the periphery. A CT angiography of whole abdomen was performed and the images were evaluated using multiplanar reconstruction and 3D volume rendering techniques. The CT angiography revealed multiple saccular aneurysms with thin irregular walls, arising from the abdominal aorta [Figures 1 and 2]. Two aneurysms were seen, one at suprarenal aorta and measuring 5.2 x 2.5 cm and the other involving infrarenal abdominal aorta and measuring 4.5 x 4 cm. One of the aneurysms was causing near-total compression of right renal artery, resulting in chronic renal parenchymal changes secondary to ischemia [Figure 3]. Multiple enlarged (largest 2.8 cm in short-axis dimension) para-aortic lymph nodes were identified in the vicinity of the aneurysms showing evidence of internal necrosis [Figure 4]. No evidence of any abnormally enhancing mass lesion or bowel wall thickening could be identified. Screening of thorax for aneurysms was unremarkable. A USG-guided core biopsy of the retroperitoneal (pre-para aortic) lymph node was performed. The lymph node biopsy revealed central caseous necrotic material with epithelioid cells and macrophages consistent with tubercular etiology [Figure 5]. Based on the biopsy results, a presumptive diagnosis of tubercular aneurysm was made, and the patient was put on anti-tubercular treatment and advised surgical management of abdominal aortic aneurysms. On follow-up, the patient responded well to the anti-tubercular drug therapy, as there was reduction in the size of the retroperitoneal lymph nodes including pre-para aortic and peripancreatic nodes, as compared to previous pre-treatment scans. Post anti-tuberculosis treatment, the patient was advised open surgical/endovascular stenting procedures.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old non-smoking Indian male presented with a 1-month history of chronic weakness, anorexia, weight loss, dizziness, low-grade fever (38 °C), and a pulsatile abdominal mass.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the month prior to radiological referral, the patient experienced progressive constitutional decline with weight loss, anorexia, weakness, dizziness, mild fever (38 °C), and a pulsatile mass in the abdomen.
subjective.past_medical_history: Normotensive, non-diabetic, non-smoker; no history of prior tuberculosis or intravascular procedures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for weakness, anorexia, weight loss, dizziness, low-grade fever, and a pulsatile abdominal mass.

objective.physical_examination: Normotensive, mild fever (38 °C), and a palpable pulsatile abdominal mass.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 20,000/mm^3 (normal: 3,000–11,000/mm^3), elevated CRP, positive tuberculin skin test, and negative bacterial and fungal blood cultures. Abdominal ultrasound and color Doppler showed mild hepatosplenomegaly, enlarged necrotic conglomerate retroperitoneal/periportal/peripancreatic lymph nodes, and multiple abdominal aortic aneurysms with central pulsatile flow and peripheral mural thrombus.
objective.advanced_workup: Whole-abdomen CT angiography with 3D reconstruction demonstrated two thin-walled irregular saccular mycotic aneurysms of the abdominal aorta: a 5.2 × 2.5 cm suprarenal aortic aneurysm and a 4.5 × 4.0 cm infrarenal aortic aneurysm causing near-total right renal artery compression and right renal ischemia, surrounded by enlarged centrally necrotic para-aortic lymph nodes (up to 2.8 cm short axis); thoracic screening was normal. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of a pre-/para-aortic retroperitoneal lymph node revealed central caseous necrosis with epithelioid cells and macrophages.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Ultrasound-guided para-aortic lymph node core biopsy demonstrating caseous necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis alongside a positive tuberculin skin test confirmed tuberculous retroperitoneal lymphadenitis complicated by contiguous multiple saccular tuberculous mycotic aneurysms of the suprarenal and infrarenal abdominal aorta. Anti-tubercular therapy resulted in marked regression of the retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and the patient was advised to undergo definitive open or endovascular aortic aneurysm repair.
